title: The Inflation Problem for Teachers
author: Chad Aldeman
summary: Chad Aldeman examines the specific vulnerability of teacher salaries to sudden inflation shocks, using the Wall Street Journal's report that inflation hit an annual rate of 4.2% in May 2026 -- the highest since the COVID/ESSER period -- as a prompt. Unlike private-sector workers whose wages can be renegotiated relatively quickly, teachers typically work under multi-year contracts that lock in salary levels well before inflation data is available, leaving them exposed to sudden purchasing-power declines that can persist for months or years before salary schedules have a chance to adjust. Using Bureau of Labor Statistics data graphed over the most recent decade, Aldeman shows that teacher salaries lagged inflation significantly during the 2021-2022 spike, then caught up during 2023-2025 as inflation subsided. With inflation now rising again -- driven in part by the war with Iran and higher gasoline prices -- teachers face a familiar squeeze: the good news is that salaries historically do catch up once inflation stabilises, but the bad news is that the catch-up lag means teachers absorb real purchasing-power losses for an extended period before salary schedules can respond.
points: * Multi-year contracts are the structural source of teacher salary vulnerability: salaries are locked in before inflation data is known, creating a systematic lag whenever inflation spikes suddenly. * The historical pattern is clear: teacher salaries lagged inflation sharply during 2021-2022, recovered during 2023-2025, and now face another squeeze as inflation rises toward 4.2% in mid-2026. * The Red for Ed movement's salary gains (2018-2019) illustrate how labour organising can temporarily close the salary-inflation gap, but those gains were wiped out by the COVID inflation shock within two years. * The lag dynamic compounds: each inflation period that teachers absorb creates a baseline from which the next salary cycle must catch up, meaning repeated spikes can create sustained real-wage declines. * The policy implication is not addressed in this article but is implied: multi-year contract structures may need adjustment mechanisms (inflation triggers, cost-of-living escalators) to protect teachers from macro-economic shocks they cannot individually influence.
quotes: The Wall Street Journal reported this week that inflation hit an annual rate of 4.2% in May, the highest it has been since the COVID/ESSER hike from a few years ago.

They write that, 'inflation outpaced year-over-year wage gains in May for the second month in a row. Inflation-adjusted hourly earnings declined 0.7% on the year in May after dropping 0.3% in April... That means households' purchasing power isn't keeping up with increases in the cost of things like rent, groceries and gasoline.'

Unlike many private-sector workers, teachers often work under multi-year contracts that lock in salaries well before anyone knows what inflation will be. That can leave them vulnerable to sudden shocks.

Over the long, long-term, the average teacher salary has mostly kept up with inflation, but no more than that. And teacher salaries tend to lag behind inflation increases. Once inflation comes down, teacher salaries have a chance to catch up.

Starting from left to right, you can see that teacher salaries were not growing very fast in 2016 and 2017. But then the 'Red for Ed' movement started winning larger salary increases in 2018 and 2019, and those kicked in in 2019 and 2020.

The good news is that teacher salaries have historically caught up once inflation stabilizes. The bad news is that when inflation rises suddenly, teachers often spend months or even years absorbing the hit before salary schedules have a chance to adjust.
